extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, documentaries, and Tig Notaro (readers of culture/entertainment journalism)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and implicit standards for reviewing or making a documentary about a stand-up comedian, with attention to how comedic performance, personal trauma, and directorial choices are presented. Focuses on what makes stand-up material land and how a film represents unseen performances and personal recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candid, attention-grabbing opening in stand-up
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hello. Good evening. Hello. I have cancer. How are you?” — beginning a set with a blunt personal revelation can be a defining, attention-grabbing comic choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents Notaro’s Largo opening as an example of a set that immediately establishes tone and stakes and that can push a comedian into a new level of recognition; such candor can be decisive for career and audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience connection as a measure of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing meant being in a room full of people whose laughter communicated, “I get you.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful stand-up is signaled by an empathetic response from the crowd; the reviewer treats that felt recognition (rather than simply ticket sales or media attention) as a core criterion of comedic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude and tone suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: “Comedy is a world where attitude matters; some of Notaro’s early attempts to find the right way to talk to an audience about her bilateral mastectomy are painful to watch.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece treats the comedian’s attitude and tone toward sensitive material as a quality dimension — getting the tone wrong makes material uncomfortable rather than funny. Editors/reviewers should note when attempts to address trauma feel miscalibrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing material across different venues (iterative refinement)
rubrics_metrics.description: We see Notaro trying out the line at venues around the country — it may bomb in Kansas City, but if it gets a laugh at Largo, it will mean Notaro has her comedy groove back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A laugh’s value depends on context; comedians should workshop jokes in multiple rooms. Reviewers should consider how material fares across audiences and whether a single successful venue can legitimately be used as the performance’s proxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary should ideally show the pivotal performance footage
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s a lot of talk about a comedy set that we don't see (no video exists of the now famous Largo gig) and a lot of buildup to another show... that isn’t going to be part of the film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of key footage is a notable directorial limitation; reviewers should call out when a film relies on recounting rather than showing crucial events, and filmmakers should consider how omission affects credibility and viewer engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directorial strategy: using one joke as a proxy for a whole performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors Kristina Goolsby and Ashley York make one joke serve as a proxy for the entire performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a deliberate editorial choice — effective when it captures the essence of a set, but also a potential compression/shortcut. Reviewers should assess whether such a proxy fairly represents the comedian’s work or oversimplifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative focus on recovery from illness and grief
rubrics_metrics.description: The documentary points a camera at Notaro while she figures out how to recover from all that (cancer, infections, bereavement, breakup).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong documentary can center on the subject’s process of recovery; reviewers should evaluate how authentically and comprehensively the film depicts emotional and practical steps toward recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of personal relationships as restorative elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Of course, when it comes to recovering from grief and illness, love helps — the courtship with Stephanie Allynne is charming and ends with them moving in together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing relationships and ordinary moments can humanize a subject and provide emotional balance; filmmakers should use such scenes to illuminate healing without sentimentalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between public acclaim and private confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when her album was No. 1, her confidence was at an all-time low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer treats mismatch between external success and internal state as an important theme; documentaries should explore that tension rather than treating acclaim as equivalent to wellbeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of family anecdotes to humanize the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Notaro laughs when members of her loving Texas family tell her she looks like Top Gun-era Tom Cruise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, characterizing anecdotes from family interactions are useful to portray personality and background; reviewers should note how these moments contribute to the subject’s relatability and emotional texture.
